key_insight: Clinical trajectories from health records and genetic correlations show a moderate match across neurological and psychiatric disorders, and both mostly align with the traditional diagnostic split.
clinical_relevance: The results suggest neurology and psychiatry may be better understood as overlapping disease domains, with a few disorders bridging the boundary and potentially benefiting from more integrated research and classification.
method: Used Delphi-2M, a transformer trained on 400,000 UK Biobank participants’ health records, to build disease trajectory embeddings.
Compared clinical similarity between 19 neurological and psychiatric disorders with genome-wide genetic correlations.
Assessed whether the two similarity measures agreed across disorder pairs and diagnostic categories.
evidence_signal: Across 19 disorders, clinical and genetic similarity showed partial convergence (Mantel r = 0.33), with both measures placing most disorders closer to their own category and highlighting the same three exceptions: multiple sclerosis, migraine, and essential tremor.
watch_item: This is an observational, correlation-based comparison from one cohort, so it does not prove causality or guarantee the same pattern will generalize to other populations or clinical settings.
paper_title: Clinical trajectories and genetic architecture across the neurological-psychiatric boundary
